lead: Unit 5 is about sensors that smell, taste and feel at the scale of a grain of rice. You will learn how a chemical, a gas or a vapour changes a resistance or a voltage, how micromachining turns silicon into a diaphragm or a channel, and how a smart sensor adds the electronics that turn a raw signal into a calibrated number on a bus. By the end you can name any biosensor by its two axes, read an ISFET curve, and size a piezoresistive pressure sensor on the back of an envelope.
about: Unit 5 moves from chemistry to the chip. Chapter 5.1 sets the vocabulary — analyte, recognition element, transducer — and classifies chemical sensors and biosensors. 5.2 and 5.3 apply that to gases and water vapour, where a resistance change or a cell EMF carries the reading. 5.4 chooses the semiconductor and oxide materials behind those sensors, and 5.5 shows how the same materials become diaphragms and channels for force, pressure and flow. 5.6 explains how those shapes are etched, deposited and packaged. 5.7 adds the electronics that turn a raw signal into a calibrated digital value, 5.8 covers flexible printed sensors and fusion of several readings, 5.9 covers solid electrolytes and surface acoustic wave devices, and 5.10 closes with biosensor classes, ISFET, IMFET and glucose sensors.

chapters.idea: A chemical sensor converts the concentration of a substance into an electrical signal, and a biosensor adds a biological recognition element in front of that transducer.
chapters.depth: Define analyte (the substance being measured), recognition element and transducer. Give the two-axis classification. By transducer: electrochemical (amperometric — current at fixed voltage; potentiometric — voltage at zero current; conductometric), optical (absorbance, fluorescence), acoustic (quartz crystal microbalance, surface acoustic wave, named only), calorimetric (heat from the reaction read by a thermistor). By biological element: enzyme sensor, immunosensor (antibody–antigen binding), microbial or whole-cell, DNA. Some syllabi call the recognition element a bioreceptor or receptor; those are the same thing. List advantages (selectivity, fast response, low sample volume) and limitations (short shelf life, drift, temperature sensitivity, fouling, need for calibration). Two lines each on the enzyme sensor and the immunosensor; keep the device details for 5.9 and 5.10.

figure.aria: A two-branch tree showing how biosensors are classified either by the transducer used or by the biological element used.

chapters.example: An amperometric glucose biosensor has a blank offset current of 5 nA and a sensitivity of 20 nA per mmol/L. A blood sample reads 4.5 mmol/L glucose. Find the output current. I = I₀ + S·C = 5 nA + (20 nA/(mmol/L) × 4.5 mmol/L) = 5 + 90 = 95 nA.
chapters.trap: Calling every chemical sensor a biosensor, or answering with the transducer when the question asks for the biological element (or the reverse). Answer both axes when the wording is open.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (sensor characteristics, sensitivity, selectivity); Unit 2 (resistance change as a signal).
chapters.leave: The detailed oxygen and hydrogen cells to 5.2 and 5.9; the FET devices to 5.10; enzyme kinetics to a biochemistry course.

chapters.idea: A gas sensor turns a gas concentration into a resistance, a current or an EMF, and each family of gases has a preferred physical effect to exploit.
chapters.depth: Oxygen: zirconia cell gives a Nernst EMF (state the principle here, full treatment in 5.9); paramagnetic sensor, because O₂ is strongly paramagnetic, uses the deflection of a dumb-bell or a pressure change in a magnetic field; electrochemical limiting-current cell. Hydrogen: palladium thin film or Pd gate MOSFET, where absorbed H changes the work function; catalytic pellistor; thermal conductivity cell. Gas-sensitive resistor (also called a chemiresistor, and known by trade names such as Taguchi sensor): sintered SnO₂ bead or thick film, oxygen vacancies on the surface, a reducing gas donates electrons and the resistance falls, a heater coil holds the bead at 300–400 °C, and sensitivity peaks at a chosen temperature. Catalytic gas detector: two beads, one active with catalyst and one inert, in a Wheatstone bridge; heat of combustion unbalances the bridge. Semiconductor junction devices: Pd/n-Si Schottky diode and MOS capacitor show a shift in barrier height or flat-band voltage.

figure.title: Gas-sensitive resistor chain
figure.aria: A gas and air mixture reaching a heated tin dioxide film whose resistance falls, feeding a divider, an amplifier and an alarm.

chapters.example: A zirconia oxygen sensor sits in an exhaust line at 700 K. Reference air is 20.9 % O₂ and the exhaust is 2.0 % O₂. Find the cell EMF. E = (RT/4F)·ln(p₁/p₂), with R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), T = 700 K, F = 96 485 C/mol. RT/4F = (8.314 × 700)/(4 × 96 485) = 15.08 mV. ln(20.9/2.0) = ln 10.45 = 2.347. E = 15.08 × 2.347 = 35.4 mV, reference electrode positive.
chapters.trap: Using log₁₀ instead of ln in the Nernst equation, or dropping the 4 in 4F for the four-electron oxygen reaction. Also forgetting that the cell output is logarithmic in pressure ratio, not linear.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 (sensitivity, transfer function); Unit 2 (thermistors, bridge circuits).
chapters.leave: Solid electrolyte conduction and the Arrhenius law to 5.9; bridge theory and instrument amplifiers to Unit 6; humidity as a special gas to 5.3.

chapters.idea: Humidity is measured by letting water vapour change a dielectric, a resistance or a dew point, and the result is reported as relative humidity at a stated temperature.
chapters.depth: Define absolute humidity (grams of water per cubic metre), relative humidity RH = 100 × (actual vapour pressure)/(saturation vapour pressure at that temperature), and dew point (temperature at which RH reaches 100 %). Capacitive polymer sensor: a hygroscopic polymer such as polyimide absorbs water, its dielectric constant rises towards 80, and the capacitance of a thin film between two electrodes rises almost linearly with RH. Resistive ceramic sensor: porous Al₂O₃ or TiO₂ adsorbs water, surface ions increase, resistance falls by orders of magnitude. Thermal conductivity sensor: two thermistors, one dry and one exposed, cool differently. Chilled mirror: optical detection of dew on a cooled mirror, accurate but slow and costly. Excite capacitive and resistive sensors with AC (about 1 kHz) to avoid polarisation and electrolysis. Calibrate with saturated salt solutions: LiCl gives about 11 % RH, MgCl₂ about 33 %, NaCl about 75 %. Quote response time, hysteresis and temperature coefficient.

figure.aria: A straight line of capacitance against relative humidity from 80 pF at 20 percent to 170 pF at 90 percent, with the measured point at 145 pF and 65 percent marked.

chapters.example: A capacitive humidity sensor is linear. It reads 100 pF at 20 % RH and 160 pF at 80 % RH. A room reads 145 pF. Find the RH. Slope = (160 − 100) pF/(80 − 20) % = 60/60 = 1 pF per % RH. Intercept = 100 − 20 = 80 pF. RH = (145 − 80)/1 = 65 %.
chapters.trap: Reading a resistive humidity sensor with a DC ohmmeter, which electrolyses the film and drifts; and extrapolating a 20–80 % straight line to 95 % RH, where the curve bends.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (resistance hygrometer, thermistors); Unit 3 (capacitive transducers, C = εA/d).
chapters.leave: The resistance hygrometer circuit and hot-wire anemometer to Unit 2; psychrometric charts to a data book; salt-solution tables to a calibration sheet.

chapters.idea: In a semiconductor sensor the material itself is the transducer, so the choice of material fixes the sensitivity, the temperature range and the selectivity.
chapters.depth: A semiconductor sensor reads a change in conductivity, in a junction barrier or in a FET channel. Materials: silicon for piezoresistors, Hall plates and photodiodes; silicon carbide and gallium nitride for hot and harsh places; metal oxides SnO₂, ZnO, TiO₂, ZrO₂, Ga₂O₃ for gas and humidity sensing, used at 200–500 °C; compound semiconductors GaAs and InP; conducting polymers such as polypyrrole and polyaniline, which work at room temperature but age; piezoelectric ceramics PZT and quartz. Junction devices: p-n diode, Schottky diode, MOS capacitor. Scaling: surface-to-volume ratio grows as 1/L, so a smaller sensor exposes more surface per atom, but 1/f noise, drift and packaging dominate below a few micrometres, and the cost per chip falls because one wafer holds thousands of dies. State the operating temperature and selectivity limits that follow.

figure.aria: A tree of sensor materials: silicon, metal oxides, conducting polymers and ceramics, each with its common sensor uses.

chapters.example: Compare the surface-to-volume ratio of a cubic sensor of side 1 mm with one of side 1 µm. For a cube, area/volume = 6a²/a³ = 6/a. At a = 1 mm = 10⁻³ m, ratio = 6 × 10³ m⁻¹. At a = 1 µm = 10⁻⁶ m, ratio = 6 × 10⁶ m⁻¹. The small cube has 1000 times more surface per unit volume, so surface reactions dominate it.
chapters.trap: Assuming smaller is always better. Below a few micrometres the drift, 1/f noise and package often decide the accuracy, not the sensor material.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (piezoresistive effect, semiconductor strain gauges); Unit 4 (Hall effect, photodiodes).
chapters.leave: The fabrication steps to 5.6; the pressure and flow devices built from these materials to 5.5; atomic-level band theory to a solid-state physics course.

chapters.idea: Micromachining turns a silicon wafer into a thin diaphragm, beam or channel, and the deflection or flow over it is read by piezoresistors, a capacitor or a heater.
chapters.depth: Piezoresistive pressure sensor: a silicon diaphragm with four ion-implanted resistors at the edges, wired as a full Wheatstone bridge, quoted in mV per volt of supply per bar. Capacitive pressure sensor: a diaphragm as one plate and a fixed plate behind it; pressure changes the gap d and hence C = εA/d, read by an AC bridge or a switched-capacitor circuit; more linear and lower power than piezoresistive but needs careful stray-capacitance shielding. Force and tactile micro sensors: a cantilever or a membrane array under a bump, giving a map of contact force. Flow micro sensors: thermal anemometer, a heater with thermopiles upstream and downstream, giving a voltage proportional to mass flow and its direction; differential-pressure micro flow sensor across a micromachined orifice; Coriolis and ultrasonic types named only. Position and speed micro sensors in one line: magnetic Hall and optical encoder versions. Acceleration and temperature micro sensors use the same diaphragm and beam process; they are covered in Unit 4 and Unit 2.

figure.title: Piezoresistive pressure sensor
figure.aria: Pressure bending a silicon diaphragm, whose implanted resistors form a bridge that feeds an amplifier and an analog-to-digital converter.

chapters.example: A piezoresistive pressure sensor has a gauge factor G = 120 and a diaphragm strain of 2 × 10⁻⁴ at full scale. Each resistor is 5 kΩ and the bridge is supplied with 5 V, with one active gauge. Find the bridge output. ΔR/R = G·ε = 120 × 2 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.024. ΔR = 0.024 × 5 kΩ = 120 Ω. For one active gauge, V₀ ≈ V_s·(ΔR/R)/4 = 5 × 0.024/4 = 30 mV.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the factor 4 in the single-active-gauge bridge output, and confusing the gauge factor of a metal foil gauge (about 2) with a piezoresistor (about 100).
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 (strain gauges, gauge factor, load cells); Unit 3 (capacitive transducers, bridges); Unit 4 (accelerometers).
chapters.leave: Acceleration and temperature micro sensors to Unit 4 and Unit 2; the etching and deposition steps to 5.6; micro actuators to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Micro sensors are built by adding and removing thin layers on a wafer, and the choice of process decides the shape, the material and the cost.
chapters.depth: Bulk micromachining: anisotropic wet etch in KOH or TMAH, where the (111) planes of silicon stop the etch and leave 54.7° sidewalls, plus an etch-stop layer such as heavily doped silicon or an SOI buried oxide; deep reactive ion etching (DRIE) gives vertical walls and high aspect ratio. Surface micromachining (also called the sacrificial-layer process): deposit a structural layer such as polysilicon over a sacrificial oxide, pattern it, then dissolve the oxide in HF to release the structure; stiction during drying is the main failure. LIGA and electroplating for tall metal parts. Deposition: thermal oxidation, LPCVD and PECVD, sputtering, evaporation, spin coating, electroplating. Lithography: spin resist, expose through a mask, develop, etch or deposit, strip; every extra mask raises cost. Packaging: anodic or glass-frit wafer bonding, dicing, die attach, hermetic sealing — one line only, with a pointer to Unit 6.

figure.title: Process flow
figure.aria: A vertical flow chart from wafer to oxidation, lithography, etch, deposition, release and finally packaging.

chapters.example: A KOH bath at 80 °C etches the (100) plane of silicon at 1.4 µm/min and the (111) plane at 0.02 µm/min. How long to etch a 300 µm deep pit, and how much does the (111) face recede in that time? Time = 300/1.4 = 214 min ≈ 3.6 h. Recession of the (111) face = 0.02 × 214 = 4.3 µm, small enough to treat the sidewall as an etch stop.
chapters.trap: Assuming KOH gives vertical walls. It gives 54.7° slopes because the (111) planes are the stop, which uses up extra wafer area; DRIE gives the vertical walls.
chapters.prereq: 5.4 (silicon and oxide materials); 5.5 (diaphragms and beams to be made).
chapters.leave: Transistor fabrication and VLSI layout to a microelectronics course; actuator principles and packaging reliability to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A smart sensor puts the sensing element, signal conditioning, a processor and a digital interface in one package, so the output is already calibrated and addressed.
chapters.depth: Block: sensing element → amplifier and filter → ADC → microcontroller or DSP → digital bus, with memory holding the calibration coefficients. Functions: linearisation, offset and temperature compensation, autoranging, self-calibration against an internal reference, self-diagnosis and fault flags, and a digital output with a unit attached. Standards: IEEE 1451 with a Transducer Electronic Data Sheet (TEDS), so a network can read the sensor's identity and calibration; buses I²C, SPI, UART, CAN, and the 4–20 mA current loop with HART superimposed. Distinguish a smart sensor from an intelligent instrument: the smart sensor carries its own processing and digital interface at the chip or module level. State the resolution and accuracy budget, and note that a digital output is not automatically more accurate.

figure.title: Smart sensor
figure.aria: Sensing element to amplifier and filter to analog-to-digital converter to microcontroller to digital bus output.

chapters.example: A pressure sensor has sensitivity 10 mV/kPa. Its amplifier has gain 100 and feeds a 12-bit ADC with a 3.3 V reference. Find the pressure change represented by one least significant bit. LSB = 3.3/2¹² = 3.3/4096 = 0.806 mV. Referred to the input: 0.806 mV/100 = 8.06 µV. Since 10 mV/kPa = 10 µV/Pa, one LSB = 8.06 µV/10 µV per Pa = 0.806 Pa.
chapters.trap: Quoting the ADC's 12 bits as the sensor accuracy. Bits fix the resolution only; offset, drift and gain error set the accuracy until the device is calibrated.
chapters.prereq: Unit 6 (signal conditioning, amplifiers, data acquisition); 5.5 (the micro sensor being made smart).
chapters.leave: ADC architectures and anti-alias filter design to Unit 6; fieldbus protocol details to an industrial automation course.

chapters.idea: Flexible sensors bend with the surface they are attached to, and fusing several sensors gives a better estimate than any one of them alone.
chapters.depth: Flexible substrates: polyimide (works to about 300 °C), PET, PDMS and paper. Conductors and electrodes are screen-printed or inkjet-printed silver, carbon and PEDOT:PSS; encapsulation matters because oxygen and moisture drift the response. Devices: printed strain gauges (including crack-based types with very high gauge factor), capacitive pressure pads with a foam dielectric, printed thermistors and RTDs, dry ECG and EMG electrodes, and sweat pH and glucose patches. Quote bend radius, cyclic fatigue life and the change in resistance after 1000 bends. Fusion: why fuse — redundancy, wider coverage, lower uncertainty; levels — data-level, feature-level and decision-level; methods — weighted average, complementary filter, the scalar Kalman filter (predict and update equations stated, no derivation), and majority voting. Only a few universities teach the Kalman derivation; a mention of Dempster–Shafer is enough otherwise.

figure.title: Weighted fusion of two readings
figure.aria: Two temperature sensors with different uncertainties entering a weighting block that produces the fused value of 30.7 degrees Celsius.

chapters.example: Two temperature sensors measure the same point. Sensor 1 reads 30.0 °C with σ₁ = 0.5 °C; sensor 2 reads 30.8 °C with σ₂ = 0.2 °C. The errors are independent and unbiased. Find the inverse-variance weighted estimate. w₁ = 1/0.5² = 4, w₂ = 1/0.2² = 25. T = (4 × 30.0 + 25 × 30.8)/29 = (120 + 770)/29 = 890/29 = 30.69 °C, which sits much closer to the better sensor.
chapters.trap: Averaging two readings 50/50 when their uncertainties differ, and forgetting that correlated errors (for example both sensors at the same temperature) are not reduced by averaging.
chapters.prereq: 5.7 (digital output, calibration); Unit 1 (error analysis and statistical treatment of measurement data).
chapters.leave: Full Kalman filter theory to a control or estimation course; printed-circuit ink chemistry to a materials course.

chapters.idea: A solid electrolyte conducts one ion and gives a Nernst EMF for the species it carries, while a surface acoustic wave device senses mass or elasticity change on a piezoelectric surface.
chapters.depth: Solid electrolytes: yttria-stabilised zirconia for O²⁻, sodium beta-alumina for Na⁺, Nafion for H⁺, lanthanum fluoride for F⁻. Ionic conductivity follows σ = σ₀·exp(−E_a/kT), so these sensors need a few hundred degrees Celsius for good response. Potentiometric mode gives a Nernst EMF (the zirconia oxygen cell of 5.2); amperometric mode with a diffusion barrier gives a limiting current proportional to concentration, which is linear and needs no reference gas. Applications: lambda sensor in the exhaust, SO₂ and H₂S sensors, CO₂ with a NASICON electrolyte, chlorine and pH. Surface acoustic wave (SAW): interdigital transducers (IDTs) on a piezoelectric substrate — quartz, LiNbO₃, or ZnO on silicon — launch and receive a wave along the surface; a delay line or a resonator. Mass loading or a viscoelastic film slows the wave, shifting the resonant frequency and increasing attenuation. Wireless passive SAW tags work without a battery and are used for torque and temperature. Only a few universities teach the coupling-of-modes design; keep it to a paragraph. Catalytic gas detectors, surface plasmon resonance (angle shift on binding) and optical chemical sensors go in one line each.

figure.title: SAW delay line
figure.aria: A 100 MHz radio source driving an input interdigital transducer, a delay path with an adsorbed film, an output transducer and a mixer that reads the frequency shift.

chapters.example: A SAW delay line runs at 100 MHz on quartz. An adsorbed film slows the surface wave by 0.10 %. Find the frequency shift, and check it against a mass sensitivity of 50 kHz per nanogram for a 2.0 ng film. For a delay line Δf/f = −Δv/v, so Δf = −0.001 × 100 MHz = −100 kHz. By mass: 50 kHz/ng × 2.0 ng = 100 kHz. The two agree, so the film thickness is still in the mass-loading regime.
chapters.trap: Applying the Sauerbrey equation (a bulk quartz-crystal-microbalance result) to a SAW delay line, and forgetting that the shift is proportional to mass per unit area, not total mass.
chapters.leave: Full electrochemistry of electrolytes to a chemistry course; SAW filter design to an RF course; SPR instrument details to a biosensing elective.

chapters.idea: Every biosensor is named on two axes — the biological element and the transducer — and the ISFET, IMFET and glucose strip are the three cases that exams ask for.
chapters.depth: State the naming rule with examples: enzyme + amperometric = glucose sensor; antibody + optical = SPR immunosensor; DNA + FET = GenFET. By element: enzyme, antibody (immunosensor), DNA, aptamer, whole cell. By transducer: electrochemical (amperometric, potentiometric, conductometric), optical, acoustic, calorimetric, FET. ISFET: a MOSFET with the metal gate removed, so the gate oxide touches the electrolyte; a reference electrode sets the bias; surface groups (Si–OH) gain or lose protons and shift the threshold voltage, giving a Nernstian slope of about 59 mV/pH at 25 °C, with drift and hysteresis as the main errors. IMFET: antibody or antigen immobilised on the gate, and the charge of the bound layer shifts the threshold; label-free but sensitive to ionic strength. EnFET: an enzyme layer over the ISFET gate, so the local pH change reports the substrate. Glucose: glucose oxidase (GOx) converts glucose and O₂ to gluconolactone and H₂O₂; the H₂O₂ is oxidised at a platinum electrode at about +0.6 to +0.7 V against Ag/AgCl and the current is proportional to glucose. Mediators such as ferrocene allow a lower operating potential and less interference. One line each on the disposable test strip and the continuous subcutaneous monitor. Normal fasting blood glucose is about 4–7 mmol/L.

figure.aria: A two-axis tree naming a biosensor by its biological element and by its transducer, with the FET branch showing ISFET, IMFET and enzyme FET.

chapters.example: A disposable glucose strip takes 10 µL of blood containing 5.5 mmol/L glucose. Each glucose molecule releases 2 electrons at the electrode. Find the total charge and the average current if the reaction is complete in 10 s. Moles = 5.5 × 10⁻³ mol/L × 10 × 10⁻⁶ L = 5.5 × 10⁻⁸ mol. Electrons = 2 × 5.5 × 10⁻⁸ = 1.1 × 10⁻⁷ mol. Charge = 1.1 × 10⁻⁷ × 96 485 = 1.06 × 10⁻² C = 10.6 mC. Current = 10.6 mC/10 s = 1.06 mA.
chapters.trap: Reversing the ISFET sign (the output falls as pH rises for an n-channel device with a fixed reference), and forgetting the 2 electrons per glucose molecule.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 (classification); 5.4 (semiconductor junctions and FETs); Unit 1 (sensitivity, selectivity, drift).
chapters.leave: MOSFET fabrication and I–V theory to an electronics course; enzyme kinetics to biochemistry; clinical glucose limits to a medical reference.
